items.title: Comparison of Data Normalization Techniques on KNN Classification Performance for Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset
items.quote: The results show that Min-Max Scaling provides a significant improvement in all metrics, with the highest accuracy of 0.8117 and ROC AUC of 0.8050. Z-Score Scaling provides good results, but not as good as Min-Max Scaling. Decimal Scaling shows the lowest performance. Statistical tests using Paired T-Test show significant differences between Min-Max Scaling and without normalization on all metrics (P-Value <0.05), while Z-Score Scaling and Decimal Scaling are only significant on some metrics, with P-Values of 0.08363 and 0.43839 respectively for accuracy and ROC AUC. Overall, Min-Max Scaling proved to be the best normalization method for improving KNN performance in diabetes classification.
items.claim: Min-Max Scaling significantly improves KNN classification accuracy and performance metrics, especially in comparison to no scaling or Z-Score Scaling, when applied to tabular data with features on different scales.

items.title: KeySight: Mathematical Analysis to Increase Speed and Accuracy of Computer Stereo Vision Systems Using Multiple Cameras with Keypoint Feature Detection and KNN Matching
items.quote: The use of keypoints was faster and provided real-time data that was used to filter out the matches between these keypoints led to more accurate results. Furthermore, cameras with higher separation between them (7 inches) were able to more accurately detect the distances to objects further away while cameras with 3 inches and 4 inches of separation could only find the distances to nearby objects accurately.
items.claim: The use of keypoints in KNN matching with stereo vision improves both the speed and accuracy of distance estimation, indicating that feature representation and selection can enhance KNN performance in spatial data, though this is in a specific application context.

items.statement: Standardising features prior to k-nearest-neighbour classification improves classification accuracy on tabular datasets with features on different scales.
items.independent_variable: feature standardisation (i.e., scaling features to unit variance)
items.dependent_variable: classification accuracy (e.g., F1-score or accuracy on a held-out test set)
items.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the gap in evidence regarding the impact of feature scaling on KNN classification in tabular data. Although E2 discusses KNN performance in stereo vision, it does not test or evaluate feature scaling in tabular data. The hypothesis is falsifiable because if a tabular dataset with features on different scales shows no improvement or a decrease in classification accuracy after standardisation, the hypothesis is refuted. The expected direction (increase) is based on the general understanding in machine learning that feature scaling prevents features with large ranges from dominating distance calculations in KNN, thereby improving the geometric representation of data in feature space.

items.statement: Feature scaling prior to k-nearest-neighbour classification reduces the influence of features with high magnitude on distance calculations, leading to more balanced neighborhood definitions in high-dimensional tabular data.
items.dependent_variable: feature influence on distance metrics (e.g., mean absolute difference in feature contributions to Euclidean distance)
items.rationale: This hypothesis focuses on a mechanistic aspect of KNN performance—how feature scaling affects the relative contribution of each feature to distance computation. While E2 does not evaluate this, it establishes that KNN performance in a spatial context is sensitive to feature representation. This hypothesis can be tested by computing the contribution of each feature to pairwise distances before and after standardisation in a public tabular dataset (e.g., from UCI or Kaggle). If the influence of high-magnitude features decreases after scaling, the hypothesis is supported; otherwise, it is falsified.

output.rationale: The experiment tests the hypothesis that standardising features improves classification accuracy in KNN on tabular datasets with features on different scales. The control condition (knn) evaluates performance without any feature scaling, while the treatment condition (knn+standardize) applies feature standardisation. The F1-score is used as the dependent variable because it directly measures classification performance in imbalanced or multi-class settings, which are common in tabular data. The three datasets represent diverse feature dimensions and sample sizes: breast_cancer (30 features, 569 samples), wine_binary (13 features, 178 samples), and digits_binary (64 features, 1797 samples), ensuring a range of scale and complexity. A paired Wilcoxon test is used because it assesses differences in F1 scores between the control and treatment conditions, accounting for the same model and dataset instances. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robust performance estimation, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and reduce variance due to stochasticity. The choice of these datasets and conditions directly addresses the gap (G1, G2) by testing feature scaling in real tabular data, unlike E2 which focuses on stereo vision.

The hypothesis concerns the influence of feature magnitude on distance metrics in KNN, specifically how feature scaling (standardisation) affects the relative contribution of each feature to Euclidean distance. To test this, we select 'digits_binary' (1797 x 64) as the dataset because it has high dimensionality and a large number of features, which amplifies the potential for high-magnitude features to dominate distance calculations. The control condition uses unstandardised KNN, while the treatment condition applies standardisation to the features before distance computation. We compute the mean absolute difference in feature contributions to Euclidean distance across all pairs of samples, both before and after standardisation. This metric directly reflects the hypothesis’s dependent variable. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare the distributions of these differences, as it is appropriate for non-normal, paired observations. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and two random seeds (123, 456) are used to ensure reproducibility and reduce variance due to randomness in data splits. The choice of 'digits_binary' ensures a high-dimensional, tabular context where feature scaling effects are most pronounced.
